prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as my sole prize part, unchanged from round 1. The chair's first question is whether the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems leave room for it. I think they do, and the room is specific. The comb made optical frequencies countable, and the 2012 prize covered single trapped ions, where the interrogated system is one particle and the measurement is limited by a single-ion signal. The lattice clock is a different solution: Lamb-Dicke confinement of a large ensemble of neutral atoms in a lattice, with the light shift cancelled at a magic wavelength, so that statistical power and accuracy are decoupled. Neither earlier prize contains that idea, and it is why neutral-atom clocks now set the stability record and why independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and other species reproduce it and compare at the 1e-18 level. That is a distinct invention with a precise concept, a demonstration and independent confirmation, which is what the criterion of a discovery or invention asks for. On timing, the clock-to-clock agreement is the maturity evidence. The redefinition of the second is a metrological decision that follows from the achievement and is not a test of it, so I would not hold the prize for it. On credit, two names map onto two separable contributions, and I would have the citation say so by naming both the invention and the realization.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 remain, and I do not claim to have removed them. First, a skeptic can still call the lattice clock the third step in one precision-timekeeping line, and the committee should write the citation tightly around magic-wavelength lattice trapping so it does not read as a general prize for optical clocks. Second, the credit is two names for a field with strong contributions from Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Schmidt and the Paris, PTB and other Boulder groups; I cannot establish from the supplied record how decisive each early contribution was, and in the Katori and Ye split the concept and the record realization are not equal kinds of credit. Third, the pending redefinition means some colleagues will see the prize as early. Finally, the prize would follow the 2025 circuit-physics award within the broader quantum-technology area, which is a point about balance, not about merit. I weigh these as real but not decisive.

responses.point: Mehlig asks why I ranked B038 as low as sixth, whether on credit or on novelty after the 2016 prize, and argues that a concept-level organising principle confirmed across HgTe, InAs/GaSb and Bi2Se3 is what the prize should reward.
responses.response: The answer is mostly credit, and then overlap. The Z2 classification is a genuine organising concept and I accept that it is the most matured of the entries I weighed against the clock, so I move B038 up to my first alternative. But the HgTe experiment that Molenkamp performed was designed from the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal, and the citation Danielsson suggests, limited to prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation in HgTe, would have to be worded so that it does not appear to write that proposal out of the story. Zhang having died makes that exclusion harder, not easier, to defend. The 3D materials are a second gap. And the 2016 prize on topological phases covers adjacent territory, so some members will see continuation. A narrower citation can handle some of this, but it turns the prize into a story with an unexplained middle. By contrast the lattice clock has a chain with no missing step between concept, realization and independent confirmation, and that is what keeps it ahead of B038 for me, not any doubt about the physics.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether the prize should reward the idea (Katori) more than the record-setting realization (Ye), since Ye's contribution was a long-term accuracy programme more than a separate invention.
responses.response: I take this seriously and have partly changed how I describe Ye's role. I no longer want to present the two as co-inventors in the narrow sense: the magic-wavelength lattice concept and the first strontium lattice clock are Katori's. But I do not think Ye's contribution reduces to engineering. Taking the clock to the 1e-18 regime required understanding and controlling blackbody shifts, lattice light shifts and collisional and many-body effects, and the many-body clock physics that followed is a scientific result in its own right. That is what turned a proposal into the instrument the other laboratories now copy and compare against. I would therefore keep two names, and I would ask for the citation to say invention and realization to carry the asymmetry honestly. If the committee judged Ye's contribution to be solely a precision programme, I would reconsider only whether a one-name prize is better, not whether a wider group is.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the clock first but asks whether recognition should wait for the redefinition of the second and whether the Paris, Boulder, Tokyo, Yb and Al+ groups are fairly represented by two names.
responses.response: On timing we agree on the reservation but not on the remedy: I would not wait, because independent comparison at 1e-18 across laboratories is already the strongest form of verification, and postponing for an outside decision lets a regulatory timetable stand in for scientific judgment. On breadth I think her question is the real weak point of the configuration. With a three-name limit I could add one more person, but I cannot identify from the record a third whose contribution is separable and decisive in the way Katori's and Ye's are. The Yb and Al+ groups confirm and extend the method; they do not supply a different idea. So I stay at two, and I register that the committee is making a judgment on incomplete priority information rather than a clean one.

responses.point: Kroll proposes that the committee decide on recusal regarding Ye because he stayed in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder and Ye's group is at JILA, while Kroll would not widen the prize beyond two names.
responses.response: I agree with not widening the prize and I do not think the Boulder stay is a reason for Kroll to step back; a documented research visit with no collaboration or personal relationship with Ye or Katori is a connection the committee can note and weigh. I would treat it as a disclosure, not a disqualification, and I would apply the same standard to my own general Japanese link. I would add that his proximity is useful, since he can speak to how decisive Ye's group's accuracy and stability results were relative to the Paris and PTB groups, which is exactly the factual point I cannot settle.

uncertainties: How the early priority and decisive contribution divide between Katori, Ye and the Paris, PTB, Boulder and Tokyo groups; I rely on recollection of the achieved uncertainties and the early timeline rather than verified figures.

Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes on the magic-wavelength and many-atom point; I think it is, but this is a judgment on which reasonable members differ.
Whether B038 could be made defensible by a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall prediction and observation, and how a missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal would be weighed.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene will be seen as secure once the pairing mechanism is better understood; I keep it only as a later alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I have no documented personal or collaborative connection to Katori or Ye, and no candidate-specific tie to B046. My general connections are to microscopy and materials physics, David R. Clarke, long-running academic exchanges with Japanese universities (Katori is at a Japanese institution), and Chalmers colleagues, including Göran Johansson, whose circuit-QED role is relevant only to B006, which I do not propose. I do not think these require recusal, and I support the committee noting them. I also take Kroll's Boulder disclosure as a matter for the committee to note, not as a reason to alter the weighting.
